keyframe_review.note: 407-409, 88,385 km2 at 93.2-99.6 E, 38.7-41.0 N (Dunhuang to Jiuquan): the right land, the wrong years. The page gives the state 400-421, with Jiuquan and Liangning added in 401 and the capital at Jiuquan 405-420, so the shape holds 401-419. The shape sits wholly inside Cliopatria's Northern Liang shape for 402-425 (all 345 of its cells), which is itself wrong in those years (see northern-liang). The infobox gives no area; ratio unavailable.

region.text: Dunhuang and the Jinchang commandery (Anxi/Guazhou side), where Li Gao rose in 400

ledger.note: 400: Li Gao proclaims the Western Liang at Dunhuang. Li Gao was made Administrator of Dunhuang. Later that year, Tang Yao rebelled in Jinchang and acclaimed him, offering the title of Duke of Liang; he 'declared a general amnesty and changed the era name in his territory'. The Sixteen Kingdoms page: 'In 400, the Chinese general, Li Gao rebelled against the Northern Liang'.

region.text: Jiuquan commandery (the gazetteer lacks Jiuquan; Jiayuguan lies 25 km from it)

ledger.note: 401: Jiuquan and Liangning join Li Gao. 'In 401, both Jiuquan and Liangning... commanderies also surrendered to him from Northern Liang.'

405: Li Gao moves the capital east to Jiuquan 'to apply more pressure on the Northern Liang'; he also allied with the Southern Liang, nominally submitted to Later Qin and sent tribute to Northern Wei.

region.text: Jiuquan commandery (the gazetteer lacks Jiuquan; Jiayuguan lies 25 km from it)

ledger.note: 420: Jiuquan falls. Li Xin was lured into attacking Guzang and was trapped; 'He died in battle, and Northern Liang forces soon captured Jiuquan.' The Northern Liang page says 'By 421, he captured their capital'.

region.text: Dunhuang and the Jinchang commandery (Anxi/Guazhou side), where Li Gao rose in 400

ledger.note: 421: the Northern Liang ends the Western Liang. 'The city eventually fell and Li Xun committed suicide in 421, putting an end to Western Liang.' The page does not name the city; the infobox has Dunhuang as the capital in 420-421, so it is read as Dunhuang. Li Bao fled to Yiwu and became a Rouran vassal; he surrendered to Northern Wei in 444. Reviewer (ea-03-d): the page has Li Xun succeed 'in Dunhuang' before 'the city eventually fell', so the city is Dunhuang; confidence raised to 3.

notes: Cliopatria row: Western Liang 407..409, one shape of 88,385 km2. (1) The state lives 400-421 on the pages; Cliopatria has three years, and its shape sits inside its Northern Liang shape for the same years. (2) Wikidata Q4186404 is shared with Cliopatria's 'Later Western Liang' (561..586, Wikipedia title 'Western Liang (555-587)'): these are two different states, 150 years apart (Li Gao's Liang at Dunhuang and Jiuquan, 400-421, and the Western Liang of 555-587 that Cliopatria's Later Western Liang rows cover); this dossier is Li Gao's only and the Later Western Liang is another dossier. (3) The infobox's preceded/succeeded fields are garbled in the fetched text; both are read as the Northern Liang from the narrative. (4) Titles: the page has Li Gao a 'Duke of Liang'; the page names Dunhuang, Jinchang, Jiuquan and Liangning only, and does not mention Gaochang, Xiliu or a 'Governor' title. (5) Vassalage (nominal, not drawn): Later Qin, Jin, Northern Wei, Liu Song, from the infobox. (6) Gazetteer: Jiuquan is not a place name there (Jiayuguan stands in); Jinchang in the gazetteer is the modern city near Yongchang, not the ancient commandery and was not used.
